body.heading: Energy stored as chemistry
paragraphs: A battery does not store electricity itself; it stores chemical energy. Inside, two different materials — the electrodes — sit in a chemical bath called an electrolyte. The materials are chosen because one holds electrons loosely and the other attracts them strongly.

Left alone, nothing happens, because the electrons have no path. Connect the terminals with a circuit and the imbalance resolves itself: a chemical reaction at the negative electrode releases electrons, which travel through the circuit — lighting a bulb or running a motor — to the positive electrode. Every torch, toy and phone runs on that one-way journey of electrons.

body.heading: Around the loop
paragraphs: While electrons flow outside the battery, charged atoms called ions drift through the electrolyte inside it, completing the loop. If either path is blocked, the current stops, which is why a battery in an open circuit can sit for months keeping most of its charge.

The voltage of a single cell is set by its chemistry: about 1.5 volts for a common AA alkaline cell, and about 3.7 volts for a lithium-ion cell. Batteries for cars and laptops link many cells together to reach the voltage and capacity needed.

body.heading: Charging runs the film backwards
paragraphs: In a rechargeable battery, pushing current in from a charger forces the chemistry to reverse, restoring the original materials — like re-stretching a spring. Each cycle wears the electrodes slightly, which is why phone batteries slowly lose capacity over a few years.

The amounts are impressive for their size: a modern phone battery stores roughly the energy needed to lift a full suitcase up a hundred flights of stairs, released silently, on demand, through two small metal contacts.

description: A battery stores energy as chemistry and releases it as electricity, as electrons flow from its negative terminal.
